title: Stand-Up Comedy Pt I
summary: Part one of a two-part Stuff You Should Know episode on the history of stand-up comedy. The hosts trace the form from vaudeville and early emcees such as Charlie Case, through the Borscht Belt and the Chitlin Circuit, to the 1950s "sick comedy" wave in San Francisco, the 1960s-70s counterculture comics (Carlin, Pryor, Klein), the rise of comedy clubs (the Improv, the Comedy Store), late-night TV, HBO specials, Def Comedy Jam, Comedy Central, and comedians' sitcoms. Part two, on alternative comedy in the 1990s onward, is promised for a later episode.

segments.title: Opening and disclaimers
segments.summary: The hosts introduce the two-part stand-up comedy episode, warn about edgy material and controversial figures, and admit they cannot cover everything, such as Andy Kaufman and Zach Galifianakis.

segments.title: Vaudeville and Charlie Case
segments.summary: Stand-up traces back to vaudeville, where emcees told jokes between acts. Charlie Case, a storyteller who moved from vaudeville to a stand-up style around 1900, is cited as a possible first stand-up.

segments.title: Frank Fay and early stand-up
segments.summary: Frank Fay is described as one of the first stand-up comedians, an acerbic and refined wit whose style influenced later comics. The hosts note his offensive views.

segments.title: Borscht Belt and Henny Youngman
segments.summary: The Jewish resort comedy circuit in the Catskills and Adirondacks shaped stand-up with jokes about Jewish life and self-deprecation. Henny Youngman, the king of the one-liners, is discussed, along with Jimmy Carr's darker one-liners.

segments.title: Borscht Belt legacy and Chitlin Circuit
segments.summary: The Borscht Belt lasted into the 1970s, with Mel Brooks, Jackie Mason, Sid Caesar and Jerry Seinfeld starting there. Women such as Joan Rivers and Jean Carroll broke in later. The Chitlin Circuit is introduced as the parallel venue network for Black comedians, including Redd Foxx, Flip Wilson and Moms Mabley.

segments.title: Bob Hope and mainstreaming stand-up
segments.summary: Bob Hope is credited with taking stand-up out of the resorts and into the mainstream, using a team of writers, topical current-events jokes, and touring military bases.

segments.title: Sick comedy and 1950s personality comics
segments.summary: In the 1950s a new style emerged focused on unique point of view and voice. Mort Sahl, working in San Francisco at the Hungry i, did topical political commentary. Shelly Berman's record was the first comedy album to go gold. Dick Gregory started at Hugh Hefner's Playboy Club in Chicago in 1961. Time magazine dubbed these comics sick comedians in 1959.

segments.title: Jonathan Winters, Don Rickles and Lenny Bruce
segments.summary: Jonathan Winters used character work and jokes about his mental hospital stays. Don Rickles is discussed as a fan favorite on Carson. Lenny Bruce is covered as a frank, often arrested comic whose importance to comedy and free speech is debated by the hosts.

segments.title: 1960s-70s counterculture comics
segments.summary: After Lenny Bruce, comics took more risks. George Carlin moved from clean suit-and-tie jokes to counterculture material, including the seven words routine. Richard Pryor is described as the first Black comedian to stop code switching for white audiences. Robert Klein is noted for observational and story-based humor.

segments.title: Late-night TV, Joan Rivers, Redd Foxx and Steve Martin
segments.summary: Late-night TV, especially The Tonight Show with Johnny Carson, launched careers and was a sign of respect when Carson called comics to the couch. Joan Rivers got her break there. Redd Foxx's raunchy albums and role on Sanford and Son are noted. Steve Martin is described as the first comedy superstar before walking away from stand-up.

segments.title: Robin Williams, cable specials and HBO
segments.summary: Robin Williams rose through Happy Days and Mork and Mindy and kept doing stand-up. The hosts discuss how cable let comics say more and perform hour-long specials. HBO's first comedy special was Robert Klein's in 1975, and the HBO Young Comedians specials ran from 1976 to 1995.

segments.title: Def Comedy Jam and Black comedy on HBO
segments.summary: Def Comedy Jam, produced by Russell Simmons and hosted by Martin Lawrence, launched many Black comedians on HBO in the 1990s and led to the Kings of Comedy tour and 2000 film.

segments.title: Comedy Central and early clip shows
segments.summary: Comedy Central began in 1991 as a channel of stand-up clip shows. The hosts mention shows like Chappelle's Show and Dr. Katz, Professional Therapist.

segments.title: Saturday Night Live and comedian-driven sitcoms
segments.summary: Saturday Night Live launched stars such as Eddie Murphy and Chris Rock, whose specials Delirious and Raw are discussed. Comedian-based sitcoms such as Seinfeld, The Drew Carey Show, The Jamie Foxx Show, Bernie Mac, The Norm Show, Whitney and Mulaney are covered, along with Louis C.K. and The Sarah Silverman Program.

segments.title: Other comedians from the 80s and 90s
segments.summary: Other comics mentioned include Gallagher, Carrot Top, Jeff Dunham, Andrew Dice Clay, Dennis Leary, and Tig Notaro, along with sitcoms like Mad About You, Roseanne and Home Improvement.

segments.title: Sign-off and part two preview
segments.summary: The hosts mention the Joan Rivers Ginger Rogers quote, say part two will cover alternative comedy in the 1990s, and invite listeners to email favorite comedians and jokes.
